content.text:
The benchmark runs and substantiates the performance story honestly:

| Size | Distribution | RadixSort | Arrays.sort | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1K | full-range | 0.032 ms | 0.029 ms | 0.92× |
| 1K | 0..1000 | 0.024 ms | 0.031 ms | 1.30× |
| 100K | full-range | 0.52 ms | 4.61 ms | **8.95×** |
| 1M | full-range | 5.11 ms | 54.1 ms | **10.58×** |
| 1M | signed | 4.99 ms | 53.5 ms | **10.71×** |

The results are consistent with the design: at 100K–1M elements it's **~7–11× faster** than the JDK's dual-pivot quicksort (radix is O(n) for fixed-width ints vs O(n log n)), and at 1K it's roughly at parity — the insertion-sort fast path keeps small inputs from regressing. (Standard microbenchmark caveat: these are rough, machine-specific figures, not lab-grade numbers.)
